newsitem.title: USA: Hispanic marketplace seen as a missed opportunity.
newsitem.headline: Hispanic marketplace seen as a missed opportunity.

text.p: A majority of the nation's top companies are missing opportunities to take greater advantage of the fast growing, $300 billion Hispanic market, according to a study released Friday.
Hispanics currently make up 11 percent of the U.S. population, with their numbers growing at five times the rate of the general population.

However, according to the study by the Phoenix-based National Hispanic Corporate Council, companies are not currently doing enough to target this community, which should have spending power topping $1 trillion by 2010.

Conducted with the Gallup Organisation, the study shows "companies within the sample of top 1,000 corporations appear to be confused with regards to the value of the Hispanic market," said Dr. Gabriel Gonzalez Molina, president of the Gallup Institute of Latin America.

"The study also shows that more companies than we would anticipate are either ignoring sales efforts to the Hispanic market or inadequately tracking or measuring sales to this high-growth market segment," Gonzalez Molina said.

It is a mistake for companies to think of the Hispanic market as having only one focus, said Dr. Louis Olivas, dean of the National Hispanic Corporate Council Institute, the organisation's educational arm.

"A general market approach is not appealing to the entire community -- it must be segmented," he said from McDonald's Corp. headquarters in Oak Brook, Ill., where the institute will be holding seminars next week.

"Second or third generation Hispanics have very strong cultural ties ... people carry customs and traditions from their parents. You don't sell to my household. You sell to my community," Olivas said.
And, be that community Mexican, Dominican, Cuban or Peruvian, the focus and cultural perspective of each are unique.

Of the 303 senior executives interviewed as part of the study, 36 percent said their companies targeted the U.S. Hispanic market as part of their marketing goals. Of those that do not target this segment, only 2 percent said their companies track sales to the Hispanic market.
In terms of recruiting and hiring, less than a third, 29 percent, said their companies have a formal employment goal aimed at Hispanics.
In community involvement, only 1 percent of executives said their companies contribute to national Hispanic organisations and only 4 percent contribute to local Hispanic organisations.
Most respondents within the top 1,000 corporations indicated that their companies did not have a goal or a forecast for growth in Hispanic market penetration.
"How can you avoid a market that is going to triple?," Olivas said.
When reaching the Hispanic market, the most popular approach was through newspapers, sponsored events, radio and television.

Only one fifth of the respondents said their companies used dedicated Hispanic advertising agencies while about 25 percent of the sample noted that they target the Hispanic market through mainstream advertising agencies.

The companies that seem to be doing a good job of targeting appear to be succeeding by combining marketing, human relations and community involvement with regards to the Hispanic market, Gonzalez Mollina said.
The key to the Hispanic market, Olivas said, is, "Hook my heart, hook my mind and I'll buy it."
